cloze.text: In Maslow's hierarchy, {{c1::physiological}} needs are basic survival needs such as food, water, and sleep.
cloze.extra: e.g., a patient struggling to afford groceries may not prioritize brushing twice a day. Unmet lower needs explain why some patients may not prioritize oral health.

cloze.text: In Maslow's hierarchy, {{c1::safety}} needs are personal security, housing, and financial stability.
cloze.extra: e.g., a patient who has just lost their job may cancel dental appointments due to cost concerns.

cloze.text: In Maslow's hierarchy, {{c1::love and belonging}} needs are social relationships, support, and acceptance.
cloze.extra: e.g., a teen may start brushing better to avoid embarrassment around friends.

cloze.text: In Maslow's hierarchy, {{c1::esteem}} needs are confidence, self-worth, and respect.
cloze.extra: e.g., a patient wants whiter teeth to feel better about their appearance and gain confidence.

cloze.text: In Maslow's hierarchy, {{c1::self-actualization}} is reaching full potential and personal growth.
cloze.extra: e.g., a patient values their health and is committed to lifelong prevention and learning.

cloze.text: The {{c1::Plaque Index (PlI)}} of Silness and Löe measures the {{c2::thickness}} of plaque at the {{c3::gingival margin}}.
cloze.extra: For all plaque indices on this page: higher scores = poorer hygiene.

cloze.text: Plaque Index (PlI): {{c1::all}} teeth are examined; plaque is detected with a {{c2::probe}} at the gingival margin.
PlI scoring: 0 = no plaque; 1 = plaque detected {{c1::only by probe}}; 2 = moderate accumulation {{c2::visible to the naked eye}}; 3 = {{c3::heavy plaque covering the entire area}}.
PlI calculation: scores are averaged {{c1::per tooth surface}}, then averaged {{c2::across all assessed teeth}}.
PlI interpretation: 0 = {{c1::excellent}}; 0.1–0.9 = {{c2::good}}; 1.0–1.9 = {{c3::fair}}; 2.0–3.0 = {{c4::poor}}.
The {{c1::Plaque Control Record (PCR)}} measures the {{c2::percentage of tooth surfaces}} with plaque.
PCR technique: {{c1::all}} teeth; {{c2::disclosing solution}} is applied to all surfaces and surfaces with plaque are counted.
PCR: each tooth is divided into {{c1::four}} sections ({{c2::M, D, F, L}}) — or into six.
PCR formula: ({{c1::plaque surfaces ÷ total surfaces}}) × 100%.
cloze.extra: Higher score = poorer hygiene.

cloze.text: The {{c1::Patient Hygiene Performance (PHP)}} index measures {{c2::plaque removal success}}.
The PHP and the OHI-S both examine the same six teeth: {{c1::#3, 8, 14, 19, 24, 30}}.
PHP technique: plaque is disclosed with {{c1::disclosing solution}}; each tooth is divided into {{c2::five}} sections and sections with plaque are counted.
PHP scoring: 0 = no debris; 1–5 = debris in {{c1::that number of sections (1 to all 5)}}. Scores are added and divided by the {{c2::number of scored teeth}}.
cloze.extra: e.g., plaque on 3 of 5 sections = tooth score 3.

cloze.text: The {{c1::Oral Hygiene Index Simplified (OHI-S)}} measures {{c2::debris and calculus}} accumulation.
OHI-S technique: tool = {{c1::explorer}} (probe); debris and calculus are {{c2::scored separately}}, then {{c3::summed}} for the total OHI-S.
OHI-S Debris Index: 0 = no debris; 1 = debris covering {{c1::<1/3}} of tooth; 2 = {{c2::1/3 to 2/3}}; 3 = {{c3::>2/3}}.
OHI-S Calculus Index: 1 = {{c1::supragingival}} calculus covering <1/3 of exposed tooth; 2 = calculus covering 1/3–2/3; 3 = calculus covering >2/3 of exposed tooth.
Interpretation of DI-S or CI-S (each 0–3): 0.0–0.6 = {{c1::good}}; 0.7–1.8 = {{c2::fair}}; 1.9–3.0 = {{c3::poor}} oral hygiene.
Interpretation of total OHI-S (0–6): {{c1::0.0–1.2}} = good; {{c2::1.3–3.0}} = fair; {{c3::3.1–6.0}} = poor oral hygiene.
The {{c1::Gingival Index (GI)}} measures gingival {{c2::inflammation, color, consistency, and bleeding}}.
GI technique: selected teeth; a {{c1::probe}} is used gently on {{c2::four}} surfaces per tooth (M, D, B, L).
GI scoring: 0 = normal gingiva; 1 = {{c1::mild}} inflammation, slight color change, {{c2::no bleeding}}; 2 = {{c3::moderate}} inflammation, redness, edema, {{c4::bleeding on probing}}.
GI score 3 = {{c1::severe}} inflammation, marked redness, {{c2::ulceration}}, {{c3::spontaneous}} bleeding.
GI interpretation (higher = more severe gingivitis): 0.1–1.0 = {{c1::mild}}; 1.1–2.0 = {{c2::moderate}}; 2.1–3.0 = {{c3::severe}} gingivitis.
cloze.extra: Scores are averaged per tooth surface, then across all assessed teeth.

cloze.text: The {{c1::Sulcus Bleeding Index (SBI)}} measures bleeding and tissue response to {{c2::gentle sulcus probing}}.
cloze.extra: Technique: selected teeth; probe; four surfaces (M, D, B, L) per tooth probed gently.

cloze.text: SBI scoring runs from 0 to {{c1::5}}; score 1 = {{c2::apparently healthy gingiva}} with bleeding on probing.
cloze.extra: 0 = healthy; no bleeding on probing.

cloze.text: SBI scores are averaged for {{c1::all bleeding sites}}; higher scores = {{c2::greater inflammation}}.
The {{c1::Gingival Bleeding Index (GBI)}} measures the presence of bleeding in the gingiva using {{c2::unwaxed floss}} on all teeth.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: "B for Bleeding, B for Between the teeth" — floss goes between the teeth (a probe goes around the teeth).

cloze.text: GBI and EIBI scoring: 0 = {{c1::absence}}, 1 = {{c2::presence}} of bleeding; result = (bleeding sites ÷ total sites) × 100%.
cloze.extra: Higher percentage = greater inflammation.

cloze.text: The {{c1::Eastman Interdental Bleeding Index (EIBI)}} measures interdental bleeding in all interdental areas using a {{c2::wooden interdental cleaner}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: "E for Eastman, E for Edge of the stick."

cloze.text: The {{c1::Community Periodontal Index (CPI)}} was developed by the {{c2::WHO}}; the {{c3::Periodontal Screening and Recording (PSR)}} was developed by the {{c4::ADA}}.
CPI and PSR are adaptations of the {{c1::CPITN}} used to measure the {{c2::periodontal status}} of a community.
CPI/PSR technique: {{c1::all}} teeth are examined, divided into {{c2::six sextants}}.
CPI/PSR code 3 = colored band {{c1::partially visible}}, pocket {{c2::3.5–5.5 mm}}.
CPI/PSR code 4 = colored band {{c1::not visible}}, pocket {{c2::>5.5 mm}}.
CPI/PSR codes 0–2 all have the band fully visible: 0 = no bleeding; 1 = {{c1::bleeding on probing}}; 2 = {{c2::calculus and/or defective margins}}.
In CPI/PSR, the {{c1::highest}} code per sextant is recorded — not averaged or added.
cloze.extra: Quick because it uses just one score per sextant (the highest, worst score), helping clinicians triage who needs care.

cloze.text: The asterisk (*) modifier, used only in {{c1::PSR}}, indicates {{c2::furcation involvement, mobility, recession, or mucogingival involvement}}.
CPI/PSR: higher codes = greater periodontal disease and {{c1::treatment need}}.
cloze.extra: Example: sextant scores 2, 0, 3, 1, 2, 4 — the most concerning sextant is the Code 4 one, which requires comprehensive periodontal treatment.

cloze.text: {{c1::Dean's Fluorosis Index}} assesses the severity of dental fluorosis caused by {{c2::excessive fluoride during tooth development}}.
Dean's Fluorosis Index technique: all erupted teeth are examined {{c1::visually with good lighting}}; the score is the most severe form of fluorosis that appears on {{c2::two or more}} teeth.
cloze.extra: Higher scores = greater severity of fluorosis.

cloze.text: Dean's index: Questionable (0.5) = {{c1::a few white flecks or spots}}.
cloze.extra: Normal (0) = no sign of fluorosis.

cloze.text: Dean's index: Very mild (1) = white areas affecting {{c1::<25%}} of the tooth surface; Mild (2) = white opacities affecting {{c2::<50%}}.
Dean's index: {{c1::Moderate (3)}} = all tooth surfaces show white areas with some brown stains.
Dean's index: {{c1::Severe (4)}} = brown stains, pits, and surface damage on most or all teeth.
{{c1::DMFT/DMFS}} (Decayed, Missing, Filled Teeth/Surfaces) measures {{c2::cumulative caries experience}} in permanent teeth.
DMFT/DMFS examines all permanent teeth ({{c1::third molars}} excluded) with an {{c2::explorer}}.
In DMF, M = missing {{c1::due to caries}} — extractions for other reasons are excluded.
cloze.extra: D = decayed (active caries present); F = filled due to previous caries. Final score = D + M + F.

cloze.text: Program evaluation with DMF/dmf: a reduction of D (or d) and increase in F (or f) = {{c1::successful caries treatment program}}; an increase in D (or d) = {{c2::failure of caries prevention program}}.
{{c1::dmft/dmfs}} and {{c2::deft/defs}} measure caries experience in {{c3::primary}} teeth.
cloze.extra: Tool: explorer. t = teeth; s = surfaces.

cloze.text: In deft/defs, "e" = {{c1::extraction needed (due to decay)}}; {{c2::missing}} teeth are not considered.
cloze.extra: Final score = d + e + f.

cloze.text: Mixed dentition: record {{c1::DMFS/DMFT}} for permanent teeth and {{c2::dmfs/dmft}} for primary teeth, separately.
In the dmf/def indices, a tooth with both decay and a filling is scored as {{c1::"d" (decayed)}}.
cloze.extra: Higher d = caries count/need for treatment; higher e or m = need for education and earlier intervention; higher f = better dental utilization.

cloze.text: {{c1::dft/dfs}} are modifications for primary teeth that count only decayed and filled teeth/surfaces (final = d + f) — {{c2::no scoring for missing or extraction}}.
cloze.extra: Higher d = caries count, need for treatment; higher f = better dental utilization.

cloze.text: The {{c1::Root Caries Index (RCI)}} measures total root caries experience; decay is counted on {{c2::exposed roots}} of all permanent teeth (third molars excluded) with an explorer.
RCI formula: ({{c1::decayed + filled root surfaces}}) ÷ ({{c2::total exposed root surfaces}}) × 100.
cloze.extra: D: higher count = higher disease, need for treatment; F: higher count = better dental utilization.

cloze.text: {{c1::Early Childhood Caries (ECC)}} = one or more dmfs ({{c2::cavitated or noncavitated}}) in a child younger than {{c3::6}} years.
cloze.extra: ECC/S-ECC: all primary teeth, visual detection; evaluates a child's primary dentition from birth to 6.

cloze.text: Severe ECC (S-ECC) in a child younger than 3 years = {{c1::any smooth-surface caries}}.
S-ECC from age 3 to 6 = ≥1 cavitated lesion in the {{c1::maxillary anteriors}}, OR a dmfs of ≥{{c2::4}} (age 3–4), ≥{{c3::5}} (age 4–5), ≥{{c4::6}} (age 5–6).

basic.back: An index that measures the presence or absence of a condition
An index that measures all evidence of past occurrences of a condition
An index that measures a dental condition that cannot be reversed
An index that measures a dental condition that can be reversed
The index rules are easy to understand
basic.extra: e.g., the Plaque Index clearly defines scores from 0 (no plaque) to 3 (abundant plaque).

basic.back: The index is easy to apply in clinical or field settings
basic.extra: e.g., the OHI-S uses only six teeth for quick evaluation.

basic.back: The criteria are not open to interpretation
basic.extra: e.g., the DMFT index (Decayed, Missing, Filled Teeth) uses straightforward clinical findings.

basic.back: The index measures what it is intended to measure
basic.extra: e.g., the Gingival Index is designed specifically to assess the severity of gingivitis.

basic.back: The index produces consistent results across different examiners or conditions
basic.extra: e.g., trained and calibrated clinicians using the Community Periodontal Index (CPI) report similar scores.

basic.back: The data can be recorded numerically
basic.extra: e.g., a Plaque Index score of 2.0 can be tracked and compared over time.

basic.back: The index can detect small changes in health status
basic.extra: e.g., a plaque control record shows even slight improvements in oral hygiene between visits.

basic.back: The index does not cause harm or discomfort to the patient
basic.extra: e.g., disclosing tablets used to highlight plaque are safe and easy to use.

basic.back: Describes traits that can't be measured numerically
Data based on numbers that can be counted or measured
Groups items into named categories with no numeric meaning
Measured on a numeric scale; can take any value, including decimals/fractions
basic.extra: e.g., probing depth, plaque score percentage

basic.back: Data with only two possible options
Categories that can be ranked in order, but the differences between ranks aren't necessarily equal
basic.extra: e.g., gingival index — mild, moderate, severe inflammation

basic.back: Data that comes in whole numbers only

basic.front: Why is the SBI considered more comprehensive than the GI?
basic.back: It shows not just whether bleeding occurs but also how inflamed the tissue is.

basic.front: When is the dft/dfs best used instead of the dmft/deft?
basic.back: When it's unclear whether missing primary teeth were lost naturally or due to decay.

typein.question: Plaque Index (PlI): into how many sections is each tooth divided? (number)
PlI: a tooth scores 1, 2, 1 and 0 on its four surfaces. What is the tooth score? (number)
typein.extra: (1+2+1+0)/4 = 1. Final PlI = average of all teeth.

typein.question: PCR: a patient has 24 teeth (4 surfaces each) and 48 surfaces with plaque. PCR score? (%)
typein.extra: 24 × 4 = 96 surfaces; 48/96 × 100 = 50%. (The book also writes "28 × 4 = 96" — a typo; 24 × 4 = 96.)

typein.question: PHP: six teeth score 3, 2, 4, 1, 2, 5. Final PHP score? (2 decimals)
typein.extra: (3+2+4+1+2+5)/6 = 17/6 = 2.83. Higher = poorer hygiene. (The book calls this the PHP-M score.)

typein.question: What is the maximum possible total OHI-S score? (number)
typein.extra: Debris Index max 3 + Calculus Index max 3.

typein.question: OHI-S: debris scores 1, 2, 0, 1, 3, 2; calculus scores 0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 3. Total OHI-S? (2 decimals)
typein.extra: DI-S = 9/6 = 1.5; CI-S = 8/6 = 1.33; total = 2.83 (fair). 6 = number of teeth.

typein.question: GI: a tooth scores 1, 2, 0 and 1 on its four surfaces. Tooth score? (1 decimal)
typein.extra: (1+2+0+1)/4 = 1.0. The final GI is the average of all teeth assessed.

typein.question: SBI: five teeth score 2, 1, 3, 1, 0. Final SBI? (1 decimal)
GBI: after inserting unwaxed floss, how many seconds do you wait to observe bleeding? (number)
GBI: 7 of 28 interdental sites bleed. GBI score? (%)
EIBI: after inserting the wooden interdental cleaner, how many seconds until you check for bleeding? (number)
EIBI: 3 of 10 interdental areas bleed. EIBI score? (%)
A patient has 3 decayed teeth, 2 missing (due to caries) and 4 filled. DMFT? (number)
A child has 2 decayed teeth, 3 needing extraction (due to caries) and 5 filled. deft? (number)
A child has 3 decayed and 4 filled primary teeth. dft? (number)
Root Caries Index: how many root surfaces are scored per tooth? (number)

mcq.question: A long-time recall patient was recently evicted from her apartment and has missed her last two appointments, saying she is "just trying to find a place to stay." Which level of Maslow's hierarchy is most likely unmet?
mcq.explanation: Safety needs = personal security, housing and financial stability. Until housing is secure she is unlikely to prioritize oral health. Esteem (confidence, self-worth) is a higher level and is not what is threatened here.

mcq.question: Which of the following is an IRREVERSIBLE index?
mcq.explanation: An irreversible index measures a condition that cannot be reversed — dental caries (DMFT). Gingival inflammation (GI, SBI) and plaque (PlI) can be reversed, so those are reversible indices.

mcq.question: Three calibrated hygienists independently score the same patient with an index and obtain nearly identical results. Which criterion of an ideal index does this demonstrate?
mcq.explanation: Reliability = consistent results across different examiners or conditions. Validity is whether the index measures what it is intended to measure — examiners can agree perfectly on an index that measures the wrong thing.

mcq.question: An index is chosen because it detects even slight improvements in a patient's oral hygiene between two visits. Which criterion is being valued?
mcq.explanation: Sensitivity = ability to detect small changes in health status (book example: the plaque control record). Quantifiability only means the data can be recorded numerically.

mcq.question: A researcher records gingival inflammation as mild, moderate, or severe. The distance between "mild" and "moderate" is not necessarily the same as between "moderate" and "severe." These data are:
mcq.explanation: Ordinal data have categories that can be ranked in order, but the differences between ranks aren't necessarily equal. Continuous data can take any value on a numeric scale (e.g., probing depth).

mcq.question: A hygienist wants to track a patient's plaque control by disclosing ALL teeth and recording the percentage of surfaces (M, D, F, L) with plaque. Which index fits?
mcq.explanation: The PCR uses disclosing solution on all teeth, 4 (or 6) surfaces per tooth, scored as (plaque surfaces/total surfaces) × 100. PHP also uses disclosing solution but only on six index teeth divided into five sections.

mcq.question: A patient's total OHI-S score is 3.5. How is this interpreted?
options: D. Cannot be interpreted; OHI-S maximum is 3.0
mcq.explanation: Total OHI-S (DI-S + CI-S, max 6): 0.0–1.2 good, 1.3–3.0 fair, 3.1–6.0 poor. The 0–3 range applies to each component (DI-S or CI-S) on its own.

mcq.question: On probing, the gingiva around #8 is red and edematous and bleeds, but there is no ulceration or spontaneous bleeding. What Gingival Index (Löe & Silness) score does this site receive?
mcq.explanation: GI 2 = moderate inflammation, redness, edema, bleeding on probing. GI 1 has no bleeding; GI 3 requires marked redness, ulceration and spontaneous bleeding.

mcq.question: A clinician inserts a wooden interdental cleaner into each interdental area and checks for bleeding after 15 seconds. Which index is being recorded?
mcq.explanation: EIBI = wooden interdental cleaner, check at 15 sec ("E for Eastman, E for Edge of the stick"). The GBI uses unwaxed floss and a 30-second wait.

mcq.question: During PSR screening of the mandibular anterior sextant, the colored band of the probe remains partially visible at the deepest site, and there is calculus. Which code is recorded for that sextant?
mcq.explanation: Code 3 = band partially visible (pocket 3.5–5.5 mm). Only the highest code per sextant is recorded, so the calculus (code 2) is outranked by the pocket depth (code 3).

mcq.question: A child has white opacities covering about 40% of the surface of four maxillary anterior teeth, and brown staining on ONE molar. What is the Dean's Fluorosis Index score?
mcq.explanation: The score is the most severe form that appears on two or more teeth: four teeth with opacities <50% = Mild (2). The brown stain on a single molar doesn't count because it appears on only one tooth.

mcq.question: Which child meets the definition of SEVERE early childhood caries (S-ECC)?
options: A. A 5-year-old with one filling on a mandibular incisor
B. A 4-year-old with two occlusal fillings on primary molars
C. A 5-year-old with one cavitated lesion on a maxillary central incisor
D. A 5-year-old with three decayed posterior surfaces
mcq.answer: C. A 5-year-old with one cavitated lesion on a maxillary central incisor
mcq.explanation: From age 3, any cavitated lesion in the maxillary anteriors = S-ECC. The other children have ECC only: their dmfs is below the age threshold (≥5 at 4–5 y, ≥6 at 5–6 y) and none involves the maxillary anteriors (a mandibular anterior filling is ECC per the book).

mcq.question: Over five years a school sealant/treatment program sees the mean D component of the DMFT fall and the F component rise. How should this be interpreted?
options: A. Failure of the caries prevention program
C. Increased need for education and earlier intervention
D. Poorer access to dental care
mcq.explanation: Reduction of D and increase in F = successful caries treatment program (higher F = better dental utilization). An increase in D would signal failure of the prevention program; a higher M signals need for education/earlier intervention.
